notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0120e.stoa001.opp-l: The edition's bracketed source references (e.g. 'S. Greg. lib. II, ep. 36', 'Psalm. CIV') and its variant readings marked 'al.' or 'Vulg.' are apparatus and have been left out of the translation; where a variant matters it is noted here. 'Liberos' ('free men') in the list of persons barred from accusing is odd; 'libertos' ('freedmen') may be meant. 'Tergiversatio' is the legal term for abandoning or evading a prosecution. 'Mutilentur' has the variant 'ventilentur' ('aired'), which makes better sense. The sentence 'Jam perditis odium debemus operire...' is obscure and probably corrupt (variant 'operi, de cujus'); the rendering is tentative. 'Nobis' in 'dicente nobis propheta' and 'contradicunt nobis' has the variant 'vobis'. 'In honore' in the Ecclesiasticus quotation stands where the Vulgate has 'hora' ('in a swift hour'). The consul's name has the variants Constantius and Constans.

The editor's parenthetical source references (biblical, Leo, Gregory, Prosper, the Roman synod under Symmachus, etc.) and Vulgate variant readings are omitted from the translation. 'Non angustiamini in carnalibus... in spiritualibus' follows this text's deliberate alteration of 2 Cor. 6:12. 'Pro perfidia aut liberari pro venia': variant 'laborare' noted by the editor; sense uncertain. 'Laudat furem' is the text's reading for Vulgate 'potior fur quam' (Ecclus. 20:27), translated as given. 'Perceptor vel primas' read as 'perceptor ... primo possessori' (variant). Several scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. negntinntes = negotiantes, oris = ovis taken as 'oris' per main text).

Bracketed source references belong to the edition and are kept. 'Constantino (Constantio) clarissimo consule': the edition offers Constantius as an alternative. 'ad sacrilegos' is noted by the edition as perhaps to be read 'sortilegos' (soothsayers). 'Luc. i.' corrected to Luke 10. Near the start of letter III, 'nobisque viam monstrandam circa nos ... invicem caritatis indulsit' is syntactically difficult and probably corrupt; translated literally. 'et vox' before 'discite' likely corrupt (perhaps 'audite vocem'); '[hear]' supplied. In the Ecclesiasticus quotation, 'Fili, si habes' lacks its object; '[the means]' supplied.

The opening quotation (Ecclus. 15:11) reads "Per Dominum abest" here; the Vulgate has "Per Deum abest" (i.e. 'it is God's fault [that wisdom] is lacking'); rendered literally. "non retardabit sufferentis" is elliptical (Vulgate: 'the patience of the one who shows mercy will not be delayed'); [the patience] supplied. "Omnis misericordia faciet tecum" is garbled against the Vulgate ('omnis misericordia faciet locum'); translated as it stands. "in prædicto Kalendarum die" is odd after a date given by the Nones; translated literally. Evident scanning errors (implanavit, cagnoscit, caetum/cadi, u.ius, orguuntur, ncc, Dc, Jesn, etc.) silently corrected. Editor's footnote marks (1), (2) omitted.

nodes.text: APPENDIX III, ON SAINT EUSEBIUS, POPE.
FIRST LETTER,
OF POPE EUSEBIUS TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF GAUL.

1. Laymen are forbidden to accuse priests, as are those who are in any way subject to them. 2. Which accusations ought not to be heard by ecclesiastical judges, and which accusers are to be barred from accusing.
To his dearest brothers, beloved in the Lord and God, all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Gaul, Eusebius.

I received the letters of your holiness with great thanksgiving, rejoicing at your safety but deeply saddened at your oppression. As to what you asked, namely what ought to be done about converted heretics, know that those who were baptized in the faith of the holy Trinity we receive by the laying on of a hand.
I.

Concerning the accusations of clerics, about which you wrote, know that it has been kept in this holy city since the time of the apostles that accusers and accusations which the laws of outside usage do not admit are barred from accusing clerics. Likewise it has been observed and established up to now that laymen do not accuse bishops, because they are not of the same way of life. And some of them are very hostile to them, since the life and conduct of [bishops] ought to be set apart and removed from the doings of laymen. Nor ought they to be attacked by those whose chastity and gravity these are unwilling to imitate, especially since the [laymen] in turn are unwilling to accept them in their own accusations. Concerning them, namely his own husbandmen and ministers, the Lord says to laymen and to all who persecute them: Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no evil to my prophets. And holy scripture itself says: Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye. For the holy fathers, foreseeing such dangers and others like them, forbade laymen serving in the world to accuse priests; likewise they barred slaves and free men, and those subject to public or private dues, and all infamous persons, from such accusation or evasion. For it is not right that the carnal be permitted to persecute the spiritual, nor that those entangled in crimes, or serving in the world, should defame or tear at bishops or lay a charge against them. For if the apostles or their successors had permitted this, very few would have remained to serve the Lord in the priestly order. Therefore we too, following the footsteps of the fathers, for the protection of the servants of God, withdraw from all persons whom the public laws do not admit to accusation the licence to attack another. And let no accusations be heard by ecclesiastical judges which are forbidden by the laws of the world.
II.

Therefore those in whom polished perfection to the fingertip has not been instilled ought to keep silent about such matters, so that they are neither mutilated nor put forward. Nor are those who are suspect either in the catholic faith or of enmity to be admitted to arraign the aforesaid, because unbelief and enmity commonly hinder the truth of a declaration. Nor are those to be believed or admitted who of their own accord confess the crimes of others. And therefore their truthfulness must be carefully re-examined: the truth which a voice offered voluntarily cannot hold in them, a rigorous torturer must extract from its hiding places by various torments, so that while their bodies are subjected to punishments, what was done may be faithfully and truly searched out. Therefore, I beg you, turn your faces first to the public laws, then to the judges, who are able and willing to speak justly in defence of all. For shall we (whom the service of God, after the casting off of these things, has made free; who either despise or laugh at the insults or abuse of such men; to whom it is written by the Apostle about servants and common people: Remember that your Lord and theirs is in heaven) be called back to these evils of the world? Are we to do what, when another does it, we maintain is profane? Shall what would defile the sight when done by the ministry of a command and another's hand be carried out at our own order? Do not keep this mind throughout all the churches, after the manner and nature of rapacious wolves: because after the bloody inquiry perhaps stains us for their desires, they will not achieve in these men the outcome they aim at, for the prophet says to us: Let us put a ring in their nostrils and a bridle on their lips, and lead them back into the right way. For, as the same prophet asserts, those are attacked who say: They shall be as though they were not, and the men who contradict us shall perish. For beyond doubt the assailants of bishops are infamous, and all who arm themselves against the fathers, and the tramplers of the churches and of its priests, and those who flee from public battles, and despise the commandments of God, and who are sprinkled with the stains of infamy by any fault: from all these we too, following the institutions of the fathers, withdraw the licence to attack bishops; because God so hates those who persecute the fathers, as invaders of the fathers, who are branded with infamy throughout the world, and therefore are justly and according to the rules rejected. Now there is no need of long admonition. We ought now to cover our hatred toward the lost, of whom, as authors, nothing remains now that is not condemned. Of them the Lord speaks through the prophet, saying: Rejecting the word, you have hoped in calumny and in tumult, and have leaned upon it. Therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach. Again the prophet cries out about such men, saying: Come here, you seed of the adulterer and of the fornicator. Whom have you mocked? Against whom have you opened wide [your mouth] and thrust out your tongue? Are you not wicked children, a lying seed? Let the impious cease now to tell falsehoods against the simple with fraud! Keep, says the prophet, your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. The eyes of the Lord are on the just, and his ears toward their cry. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth. And a little later: Malice shall slay the wicked, and those who hate the just shall be found guilty. As for us, though we suffer much from such men, let us love one another, dearest ones, for love is from God. And everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love. In this the love of God appeared among us, that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. In this is love, not as though we had loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins. Dearest ones, if God loved us, we too ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us. In this we understand that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit. And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son, the Saviour of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God. And we have known and believe the truth which God has in us. God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him. In this love is perfected with us, that we may have confidence on the day of judgement: because as he is, so are we also in this world. There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear involves punishment. And whoever fears is not perfect in love. Let us therefore love God, because God first loved us. If anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God, that whoever loves God should love his brother too. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. And everyone who loves him who begot loves also him who is born of him. In this we have known that we love the children of God, when we love God and do his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not heavy, because everything that is born of God conquers the world. And this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith. Who is it that conquers the world, except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ, not in water only, but in water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies that Christ is the truth. For there are three who give testimony, the spirit, the blood and the water, and these three are one. If we accept the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater. For this is the testimony of God, which is greater, that he has testified about his Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself. Whoever does not believe the Son makes him a liar, because he does not believe in the testimony which God has testified about his Son. And this is the testimony, that God has given us eternal life. And this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life. I write these things to you, that you may know that you will have eternal life, you who believe in the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence we have toward him: that whatever we ask according to his will, he will hear us. And we know that he hears us, whatever we ask. We know that we have the petitions which we request of him. Whoever knows that his brother is sinning a sin not unto death, let him ask, and life will be given to him who sins not unto death. There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for that. All iniquity is sin, and there is a sin unto death. We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin, but the begetting of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him. For we know that we are of God, and the whole world lies in the evil one. And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, that we may know the true God and be in his true Son. This is the true God and eternal life. Because of their evil deeds many powerful men have been heavily oppressed, and glorious men have been handed over into the hands of others. But the blessing of God hastens as the reward of the just man, and in honour his swift advance bears fruit. Blessed is the man who has not slipped by a word from his mouth, and has not been goaded by the sorrow of transgression. Know, dearest ones, that by the piety which is owed to you as servants of God, I have graciously received all your submissions, which will benefit the catholic faith, so that by their work Christian peace may be restored and impious error abolished. And if anything further about such matters or matters like them needs to be deliberated, let a report be sent to us quickly, so that, the nature of these things having been examined, our solicitude may determine what ought to be observed. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, Constantine being consul.
LETTER II,
OF POPE EUSEBIUS TO THE EGYPTIANS.

On bishops stripped of their property or driven from their see: that they are not to be judged unless they are restored in full; on the summoning of synods: that they be heard by all the bishops of their province.

Eusebius, bishop of the Roman and apostolic Church, to the brothers most beloved in the love of Christ, of one mind, joined by the glue of love, serving the Lord throughout Alexandria and Egypt and holding the right faith: greeting in the Lord.

Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we too may be able to console those who are in any distress through the exhortation with which we ourselves are exhorted by God. For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through Christ our consolation abounds. Whether we are afflicted, it is for your exhortation and salvation, or whether we are exhorted, it is for your exhortation and salvation, which works the endurance of the same sufferings which we also suffer. And our hope for you is firm, knowing that as you are sharers in the sufferings, so you will be also in the consolation. The old things, most beloved, have passed away, and behold, new things have come about. And all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ, and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; since indeed God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their transgressions against them; and he has placed in us the word of reconciliation. So we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you on Christ's behalf: be reconciled to God. Him who had not known sin he made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. And as helpers we exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Giving no offence to anyone, so that our ministry may not be found fault with, but in all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in hardships, in beatings, in prisons, in riots, in labours, in vigils, in fasts, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering and gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonour, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful, as unknown and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and possessing all things. Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians, our heart is opened wide. You are not constrained in carnal things, but you are constrained in spiritual things. Having the same recompense, I speak as to children: open yourselves wide too. Do not bear a yoke with unbelievers. For what sharing has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what part has a believer with an unbeliever? What accord has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as the Lord says: For I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people. Therefore come out from their midst, and be separate from their midst, says the Lord; and do not touch what is unclean, and I will receive you, and I will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord almighty. Having therefore these promises, dearest ones, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. Correct your error, brothers, and guard yourselves from every stain of error, so that you may be able to offer a pure gift to God. Do not persecute the servants of God, do not defame bishops nor accuse them, because God willed that they be reserved for his own judgement. For that he did not wish them to be corrupted or accused by men of the world or of wicked life, he himself gave the example when by himself, and not through another, he cast the trading priests out of the temple, and overturned the tables of the money-changers with his own whip, and cast them out of the temple. And as he says elsewhere: God has stood in the assembly of the gods, and in the midst he judges between gods. So whoever accuses or condemns bishops accuses the ordinance of God, since he pursues spiritual things less than earthly ones. For the cause of faith and love, in which Christian salvation consists, compels me to labour with much solicitude, fearing that the depravity which ought to have been cut off at its beginnings may in the course of time become both more stubborn and more deeply rooted. For it is very hostile and unfitting that those who harass bishops or the other true priests with their persecution should be mixed without distinction with the names of catholics, since, not abandoning a condemned impiety, they are condemned by their own depravity; they ought to be struck down for their faithlessness, or set free for pardon. For as it is full of piety that the Lord's love be restored to the oppressed, so it is just that the authority of one who throws everything into confusion be cut off. I wonder, dearest ones, why you are so quickly moved and carried away from your understanding, since it is written: Do not go after your desires, and turn away from your own will. If you grant your soul its desires, it will make you a joy to your enemies. Do not take delight in crowds, nor in small ones; for their offence is at hand. Do not be poor in strife from borrowing, when you have nothing in your purse; for you will be envious of your own life. A drunken workman will not become rich, and he who despises small things will fall little by little. Wine and women make the wise fall away, and reprove the sensible; and he who joins himself to harlots will be worthless. Rot and the worm will inherit him, and he will be raised up as a greater example, and his soul will be removed from the number. He who believes quickly is light of heart and will be diminished; and he who sins against his own soul will be held of no account besides. He who rejoices in iniquity will be marked out; and he who hates correction, his life will be lessened; and he who hates talkativeness extinguishes malice. He who sins against his own soul will repent; and he who delights in malice will be marked out. Do not repeat a wicked and harsh word, and you will not be diminished. Do not tell your mind to friend or enemy, and if you have a fault, do not lay it bare. For he will hear you and watch you, and as if defending the sin he will hate you, and so he will cling to you always. Have you heard a word against your neighbour? Let it die within you, trusting that it will not burst you. Before a word the fool is in labour, like the groaning of one giving birth to a child. An arrow stuck in the thigh of the flesh: so is a word in the heart of a fool. Reprove a friend, in case he did not understand, and when he has done a wrong and did not understand, let him say: I did not do it; or if he did it, that he may not do it again. Reprove a neighbour, in case he did not say it; and if he said it, that he may not repeat it. Reprove a friend, for often an offence is committed, and do not believe every word. There is one who slips with his tongue, but not from his heart. For who is there who has not sinned with his tongue? Reprove a neighbour before you threaten, and give place to the fear of the Most High, for all wisdom and knowledge is the fear of God, and in all wisdom is the ordering of the law. There is no wisdom nor knowledge, and there is no good thought except in it. The prudence of sinners is wickedness, and in it is execration; and he is foolish who is lacking in wisdom. Better is the man who falls short in wisdom and lacks understanding in the fear of God than one who abounds in understanding and transgresses the law of the Most High. There is a sure shrewdness, and it is unjust; and there is one who utters a sure word, telling the truth. There is one who humbles himself wickedly, and his inner parts are full of deceit. For there is a just man who submits himself excessively out of great humility; and there is a just man who bows his face and pretends not to see what is unknown. And if he is prevented from sinning by weakness of strength, if he finds a time for doing evil, he will do evil. A man is known by his look, and the sensible man is known by meeting his face. The clothing of the body, and the laughter of the teeth, and the gait of a man announce what he is. There is a lying reproof in the mouth of an insolent man; and there is a judgement which is not proved to be good; and there is one who is silent, and he is prudent. How good it is to reprove rather than to be angry, and not to hinder one who confesses in prayer! The lust of a eunuch deflowered a young girl: so is he who renders an unjust judgement by force. How good it is, when reproved, to show repentance! For thus you will escape wilful sin. There is one who is silent and is found wise; and there is one who is hateful because he is forward in speaking. And there is one who is silent, not having the sense for speech; and there is one who is silent, knowing the time of the fitting moment. A wise man will be silent until the right time, but the wanton and imprudent will not observe the time. He who uses many words harms his own soul; and he who takes power to himself unjustly will be hated. There is advancement in evil things for an undisciplined man, and there is a finding that turns to loss. There is a gift which is not useful; and there is a gift whose return is double. There is a lowering on account of glory; and there is one who from humility will lift up his head. There is one who buys much for a small price, and who pays it back sevenfold. The wise man makes himself loved by his words, but the graces of fools will be poured out. The gift of a foolish man will not be useful to you, for his eyes are sevenfold. He will give little and reproach much, and the opening of his mouth is a burning. Today a man lends, and tomorrow he demands it back; and such a man is hateful. A fool will have no friend, and there will be no glory for his good things. For those who eat his bread are false of tongue. How often, and how many, will mock him? For he has not distributed with right judgement what was to be kept, nor likewise what was not to be kept. The slip of a false tongue is like one falling on a pavement; so the fall of the wicked will come swiftly. An ungrateful man is like an idle tale; it will be constantly in the mouth of the undisciplined. A proverb from the mouth of a fool will be rejected, for he does not speak it in its season. There is one who is prevented from sinning by poverty, and in his rest he will be goaded. There is one who will lose his soul out of shame, and will lose it through an imprudent person, and will ruin himself by respect of persons. There is one who out of shame makes a promise for a friend, and has gained him as an enemy for nothing. A lie is a wicked reproach in a man, and it will be constantly in the mouth of the undisciplined. The persistence of a lying man praises the thief, but both will inherit destruction. The ways of lying men are without honour, and their confusion is with them without ceasing. We admonish you, brothers, to pursue unceasingly with one another in the love of Christ what will benefit people; likewise we beseech you in the Lord to walk worthily of the calling with which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one spirit, as you were called in the one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God, the Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in all of us. But to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. Therefore he says: Ascending on high he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men. Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same one who also ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all come to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, in the wickedness of men, in craftiness for the deceit of error. For it is unjust to judge rashly concerning the hidden things of another's heart; and it is a sin to censure on suspicion one whose works are seen to be nothing but good. So the sheep which have been entrusted to their shepherd ought not to censure him (unless he has strayed from the right faith), nor can they in any way accuse him; because the deeds of shepherds are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even though they may seem rightly to deserve censure. We say these things because we have found in your writings that certain bishops in your parts have been accused by their own sheep, some, that is, on suspicion, and some on sure grounds; and that for this reason some have been stripped of their property, and some driven from their own see. Know that they can neither be summoned to a provincial synod nor to a general one, nor be judged in any matter, before everything that was taken from them has been restored by law to their possession. So first everything must be restored to them by law, and the churches which were taken from them must be returned to them with every privilege; and afterwards, not within a short space of time, but as long a space of time should be granted them as they appear to have been stripped or driven out, before they are summoned to a synod and heard by each and all of the bishops of their province. For one who has been stripped or driven out can neither be summoned to a case nor be judged, since one already laid bare has no privilege of which he could be stripped. Hence it was also decreed of old that the one who took them should restore all possessions, and everything taken, and all the fruits, to the first possessor before issue is joined in the suit. And elsewhere it is found written: Let him who has suffered violence receive everything back in the state in which it was, and let him hold securely what he possesses. And elsewhere in the synodal decrees of the fathers and the edicts of kings one reads it laid down: Everything is to be restored to bishops who have been stripped or ejected, immediately, by the ordinance of the pontiffs, and they are to be recalled completely to their places from which they departed, whatever the circumstance of the time, whether by fraud, or captivity, or the power of greater men, or by any unjust causes, they are known to have lost the property of the Church or their own goods or substance, before the accusation or their regular summons to a synod, and so on. It is also decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that whoever seizes another's property should not go unpunished, but should restore everything with multiplication. Hence it is also written in the Gospel: If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold (Luke 19). And in the laws of the world it is laid down: whoever takes away another's property shall restore what was taken tenfold to him whose property was seized. And in the divine law one reads: Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbour's boundaries. And all the people shall say: Amen (Deut. 28). Let such things therefore not be presumed without vengeance, nor practised without their own condemnation (Thus far the words of Pope Symmachus, in the council cited). Pursue peace with one another and toward all, and not the loss or injustice of anyone. But doing the truth in love, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, fitted and joined together through every joint of supply, according to the working in the measure of each member, makes the growth of the body for its own building up in love. For the rest, dearest ones, rejoice and be perfect; exhort one another, be of the same mind, have peace, and the God of peace and love will be with you (Heb. 12, Eph. 4). May the Lord guard you both now and to the day of eternity (2 Pet. 3). Amen. Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, Constantine (Constantius) being consul, a most illustrious man.
LETTER III,
OF POPE EUSEBIUS, SENT TO THE BISHOPS OF TUSCIA AND CAMPANIA.

On not admitting infamous persons to testimony, and who are called infamous persons; and on receiving heretics who were duly baptised, if they return to the faith, through the laying on of a hand; which laying on of a hand is shown to belong only to the highest priests.
To the most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout Campania and Tuscia, Eusebius.

Blessed be the Lord our God, who (Hormisdas, letter 25) through his mercy enriched the Roman Church with the priesthood of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and granted us a way to be shown concerning ourselves (because of the universal care which is ours by the privilege of that same Church) of mutual love, so that we who cleave together in firmness of faith may also be joined in the delight of longed-for conversation, whereby, while we reach as far as you through the service of letters, we may the more easily also stir your hearts to religious worship by apostolic admonitions; and while we repay to the hope of our love a kind of debt, we may show a full affection toward God. Let us therefore join, most beloved brothers, continual and humble prayers, and, supplicating our God with tears of mouth and heart, let us ask with unceasing entreaty that in teaching and in deed we may cling to him whose members we desire to be, and never turn aside by a devious path from that way which is Christ, lest we, unhappy, be justly deserted by him whom we impiously leave. This can befall us, with the help of heavenly favour, in this way: if we keep the apostolic teachings, if we keep the commands of the fathers. For our Lord says: Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him (John 14). And although these things, said in general, could suffice for us either to avoid errors or to guard catholic things, yet we know it was established by the apostles and their successors (Sixtus, sentence 250; Hadrian's collection, ch. 67) that accusations against teachers ought not to be accepted, nor foreign judgements be held (Theodosian Code, book 2, title 1, constitution 10), nor anyone be bound by the sentence of any judge other than his own (Code of Justinian, book 7, title 48, constitution 4). For Christ is the head of the Church; and the priests are vicars of Christ, who in Christ's stead discharge an embassy in the Church (Hormisdas, letter 25, already cited). Therefore whatever is done to their injury pertains to Christ, who said: Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me; and whoever despises me despises him who sent me (Luke 10). These things, brothers, are terrible, and to be considered and guarded against very diligently, both on account of those who strive to destroy themselves by greed, avarice or envy, lest they slip into the depths or fall into such evils, and on account of the persecutions of the Church and of her servants, [by those] who, according to the voice of the Truth, having eyes do not see, and having ears do not hear, nor understand the things that please God. Following therefore the apostolic rule in all things, and proclaiming all its ordinances (John, letter, in the libellus after Hormisdas letter 51; 3, question 5, 'We have established with'), for the protection of the bishops, who were called pillars of the Church by God, and of the other true priests, confirming the venerable statutes of the fathers, we establish again, with all the bishops who are with us, as we have found it decreed long ago, that murderers, sorcerers, thieves, the sacrilegious, robbers (Hadrian's collection 63, in the 2nd decree of Pope Eutychian), adulterers, the incestuous, poisoners, suspects, criminals, household servants, perjurers, and those who have committed abduction or given false testimony, or who have resorted to the sacrilegious (read 'soothsayers' by Latinius's conjecture) and diviners, and those like them, are by no means to be admitted to accusation or to testimony, because they are infamous persons and justly to be rejected, since their voice is deadly. For (Theodosian Code, book 9, title 6, constitution 3) a deadly voice ought in all matters to be forbidden rather than heard. The danger, therefore, that threatens teachers must always be guarded against and avoided with the utmost care, and they are to be borne with and protected by all, as the Lord says: What you did to one of my least, you did to me (Matt. 25). For (Hormisdas, in the rule of faith, after letter 9 and letter 51) the first salvation is to guard the rules of right faith and by no means to stray from the ordinances of the fathers. Nor can the saying of our Lord Jesus Christ be passed over, who says: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church (Matt. 16). And these things that were said are proved by the outcome of events, since in the apostolic see the catholic religion has always been kept without stain. Therefore, dearest ones, [hear] also the voice according to holy Scripture: learn to do good (Isa. 1), and to turn from evil (Prov. 16), and to be steeped in the rules of the fathers, as it is written: Son, if you have [the means], do good to yourself, and offer offerings worthy of God. Remember that death does not delay, and the covenant of the underworld, because it has been shown to you. The covenant of this world will die by death. Before death do good to your friend, and according to your strength stretch out [your hand] and give to the poor. Do not be cheated of a good day, and let not a share of a good gift pass you by. Will you not leave your sorrows and labours to others in the dividing of the lot? Give and receive, and justify your soul. Before your death work justice, for there is no finding food in the underworld. All flesh will grow old like grass, and like a leaf bearing fruit on a green tree: some are produced and others cast down; so is the generation of flesh and blood: one comes to an end and another is born. Every corruptible work will fail at the end, and whoever works it will go with it. And every choice work will be justified, and whoever works it will be honoured in it. Blessed is the man who will dwell in wisdom, and who will meditate on his justice, and in understanding will think on the all-seeing care of God; who ponders her ways in his heart and will be understanding in her secrets, going after her like a tracker and standing in her ways; who looks in through her window and listens at her door; who rests near her house and fixes a stake in her walls. He will set up his hut at her hand, and good things will rest in his hut for ever. He will set his children under her shelter and will dwell under her branches. He will be protected under her branches from the heat, and will rest in her glory (Ecclus. 14). Whoever fears the Lord will do it; and whoever holds fast to justice will take hold of her, and she will meet him like an honoured mother, and receive him like a wife of his youth. She will feed him with the bread of life and understanding, and give him the water of saving wisdom to drink. And he will be made firm in her and will not be bent; and he will hold to her and will not be put to shame; and she will exalt him among his neighbours. And in the midst of the Church she will open his mouth, and fill him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, and clothe him with a robe of glory. She will store up joy and exultation upon him, and make him heir to an everlasting name. Foolish men will not take hold of her, and sensible men will meet her. Foolish men will not see her, for she is far from pride and deceit. Lying men will not remember her, and truthful men will be found in her, and will have access even to the beholding of God. Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner, since wisdom has come forth from God. For praise will stand by the wisdom of God, and will abound in a faithful mouth, and the Ruler will give it to him. Do not say: "Through the Lord it is absent"; for what he hates, you should not do. Do not say: "He led me astray"; for he has no need of impious men. God hates every abomination of error, and it will not be lovable to those who fear him. God from the beginning established man and left him in the hand of his own counsel. He added his commandments and precepts. If you are willing to [keep] the commandments, they will keep you, and [you will] for ever keep a pleasing faith. He has set before you water and fire: stretch out your hand to whichever you wish. Before man are life and death, good and evil; whichever pleases him will be given to him. For the wisdom of God is great, and he is strong in power, seeing all [men] without ceasing. The eyes of the Lord are on those who fear him, and he himself knows every work of man. He has commanded no one to act impiously, and has given no one room to sin. For he does not desire a multitude of faithless and useless sons (Ecclus. 15). Do not delight in impious sons, if they multiply, nor take pleasure in them, if the fear of God is not with them. Do not trust in their life, and do not look to their labours. For one who fears God is better than a thousand impious sons. And it is better to die without sons than to leave impious sons. By one sensible man a homeland will be peopled, and by three impious men it will be deserted. Many other (Vulg. such) things my eye has seen, and stronger things than these my ear has heard. In the assembly of sinners a fire will blaze up; against an unbelieving nation wrath will burn. The ancient giants did not entreat [pardon] for their sins, who were destroyed, trusting in their own strength. And he did not spare their sojourning, but struck them and cursed them for the pride of their speech. He had no pity on them, destroying the whole nation, who exalted themselves in their sins. And so too the six hundred thousand foot-soldiers who gathered together in the hardness of their heart: and if one alone had been stiff-necked, it would be a wonder if he had gone unpunished. For mercy and wrath are with him; he is mighty to be entreated, and pours out wrath. As his mercy is, so is his rebuke. He will judge a man according to his works. The sinner will not escape with his plunder, and he will not delay [the patience] of the one who shows mercy. All mercy will deal with you, with each according to the merit of his works and according to the understanding of his sojourning. Do not say: "I shall be hidden from God, and who will remember me from on high? Among a great people I shall not be recognised; for what is my soul in so vast a creation?" Behold, heaven, and the heavens of the heavens, the abyss, the whole earth, and what is in them will be shaken in his sight, the mountains together, and the hills, and the foundations of the earth. And when God looks upon them, they will be shaken with trembling. And in all these things the heart is without understanding; and every heart is understood by him; and who understands his ways, and the storm which no eye of man has seen? For very many of his works are in hidden places; but who will tell forth the works of his justice, or who will endure them? For the covenant is far from some, and the examination of men is at the end. He who is lacking in heart thinks evil things (Vulg. empty things); and the imprudent and erring man thinks foolish things (Ecclus. 16). So, brothers, let no evil word go out of your mouth, but whatever is good for building up as occasion requires, that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, and anger, and indignation, and clamour, and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice. But be kind to one another, merciful, forgiving one another, as God also in Christ has forgiven you (Eph. 4). Be therefore imitators of God, as dearest sons; and walk in love, as Christ also loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God for an odour of sweetness. But fornication and all uncleanness, or avarice, let it not even be named among you, as befits saints, nor shamefulness, nor foolish talk, nor scurrility, which is not to the purpose, but rather giving of thanks. For know this, understanding that every fornicator, or unclean person, or avaricious person (which is the service of idols), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one lead you astray with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of unbelief. Do not therefore become partakers with them. For you were once darkness, but now [you are] light in the Lord. Walk as sons of light (for the fruit of light is in goodness and justice and truth), proving what is well-pleasing to God; and do not take part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather rebuke [them]. For the things done by them in secret it is shameful even to speak of. But all things that are rebuked are made manifest by the light; for everything that is made manifest is light. Therefore it says: "Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you." See therefore, brothers, how you walk carefully: not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, since the days are evil. Therefore do not become imprudent, but understanding what the will of God is. And do not be drunk with wine, in which is wantonness, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks for all things, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God and the Father, being subject to one another in the fear of Christ (Eph. 5). We therefore command you to celebrate solemnly the feast of the finding of the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was recently found, while we hold the helm of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, on the aforesaid day of the Kalends. Likewise we instruct that all heretics, whoever are converted by the grace of God and were baptised believing in the name of the Holy Trinity, be reconciled through the laying on of a hand, keeping the rule of the Roman Church. The sacrament of the laying on of a hand is also to be held in great veneration, since it cannot be performed by others except the highest priests. Nor is it read or known to have been performed in the time of the apostles by others than the apostles themselves; nor can it ever be performed, or ought it to be done, by others (as has already been said) than those who hold their place. For if it is presumed otherwise, let it be held void and empty, and it will never be reckoned among the ecclesiastical sacraments. For the rest, brothers, rejoice and exult in the Lord, so that, enlightened and strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, you may be able, with the Lord's help, to come to the pastures of eternal life and lead your own [people] there. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be always with us all. Amen. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, Constantine (or Constantius) being consul, most illustrious.
